name: Low-emissions hydrogen and electrolyzers
summary: Low-emissions hydrogen substitutes cleaner production for hydrogen made from unabated fossil fuels, using electrolysis or other qualified pathways.
useCase: An ammonia plant replaces part of its conventional hydrogen supply with contracted low-emissions hydrogen when the delivered cost and reliability meet its needs.
whyNow: Actual low-emissions hydrogen production grew 20% in 2025 to almost 1 million tonnes, according to IEA, but announced ambitions have repeatedly been cut. The announced 2030 pipeline fell from 49 Mt per year in the 2024 review to 37 Mt in 2025 and 27 Mt in 2026. This decline is a correction in expectations, not a decline in actual annual production. The important commercial gap is between announcements and committed investment backed by firm customers. Refineries and chemical plants already use hydrogen and offer a clearer substitution opportunity than entirely new applications. Electrolyzer makers benefit only if efficient plants are commissioned, utilised and paid for.

mainstream.scope: Repeat low-emissions hydrogen procurement in selected refining, ammonia and industrial clusters with infrastructure and supportive economics.
mainstream.rationale: Existing industrial demand reduces the need to create a new end use, but large cost gaps and uncertain offtake remain. Several committed projects can establish regional markets by 2030, followed by repeat projects in the early 2030s. This is conditional sector adoption; large-scale use in household heating, ordinary cars or all heavy industry is not assumed. A broad market could slip beyond 2035.

metric.name: Announced 2030 low-emissions hydrogen production pipeline
metric.scope: Global annual production proposed for 2030, as assessed in successive IEA reviews; a changing expectation, not actual output.
metric.limitations: The series shows revisions to projects intended for the same future year. It must not be displayed as realised production or extrapolated as a declining production curve. Actual low-emissions output rose 20% in 2025 to almost 1 Mt.
metric.futureNote: No defensible comparable external deployment forecast found. The separate maturity path is an analyst scenario, not measured adoption.

milestones.text: The selected current reviews do not provide a comparable annual production value retained here; no missing value is interpolated.
Early project announcements are not operating output; no comparable 2022 annual measurement retained.
IEA’s later review describes rising investment decisions during this period, but project status is more informative than a headline announcement count.
The IEA review’s announced 2030 production pipeline stood at 49 Mt per year.
The pipeline assessment declined to 37 Mt per year; actual low-emissions production nevertheless grew 20% to almost 1 Mt.
IEA cut the announced 2030 pipeline to 27 Mt per year. Committed and strongly promising projects together represented just over 6 Mt; neither number is achieved output.

tailwinds: Refining and chemicals offer identifiable existing customers rather than speculative new uses.
Domestic production can diversify dependence on fossil-fuel imports in some regions.
Electrolyzer experience, better utilisation and integrated projects can improve economics.
bottlenecks: Firm long-term buyers often will not pay the premium required for financing.
Low-cost electricity, grid access, storage and transport must be available together.
Unclear qualification rules, project delays and manufacturer overcapacity hinder investment.
watchMetrics: Commissioned output with measured lifecycle emissions, separated by production pathway.
Firm offtake and final investment decisions rather than non-binding announcements.
Delivered cost per kg at actual utilisation, electricity cost and financing assumptions.
